sourceVariantTitle: The Last Cup: A Film That Does Not Let Us Look Away
scoreRule: One point per correct answer; ten points maximum. Provisional local result only.
description: Original English B2 independent Reading draft with ten inference and transfer questions; requires later pedagogical review.

tabs.title: Reasons and Limitations
tabs.description: Find how the examples support or challenge the film's message.

tabs.title: Practical Decisions
tabs.description: Apply the ideas to realistic festival planning.

questions.q: What does the reviewer suggest when saying the film sometimes trusts images more than arguments?
choices: The film has too many interviews and not enough images.
Its cheerful soundtrack makes the opening unwatchable.
Some scenes are memorable without fully explaining the problem.
The director avoids showing rubbish until the end.
questions.explanation: The reviewer uses this episode to distinguish vivid imagery, practical constraints, measurable costs and sustained responsibility for waste.

questions.q: Why is the street cleaner's explanation especially powerful in the reviewer's view?
choices: It shows that cleaning staff are responsible for all plastic waste.
It turns a general environmental concern into a specific practical problem.
It proves that one extra bin will solve the problem permanently.
It allows the filmmaker to avoid discussing the event's budget.
questions.explanation: The reviewer uses this episode to distinguish vivid imagery, practical constraints, measurable costs and sustained responsibility for waste.

questions.q: What attitude does the director show by including the teenagers' messy first evening?
choices: She expects the audience to reject the teenagers' idea.
She argues that no concert should ever be held on a beach.
She suggests that borrowing equipment is always the cheapest option.
She treats an imperfect attempt as worth watching without ridicule.
questions.explanation: The reviewer uses this episode to distinguish vivid imagery, practical constraints, measurable costs and sustained responsibility for waste.

questions.q: How do the venue's security rules complicate the advice to bring a reusable cup?
choices: They show that an apparently simple choice may not be available to everyone.
They prove that the director had no permission to film at the venue.
They suggest the café owner is unwilling to support any environmental action.
They explain why all visitors preferred single-use bottles.
questions.explanation: The reviewer uses this episode to distinguish vivid imagery, practical constraints, measurable costs and sustained responsibility for waste.

questions.q: Why does the reviewer value the organisers' admission that the first summer was expensive?
choices: It demonstrates that reusable cups should never be introduced.
It indicates that water for washing is the only remaining problem.
It makes the solution credible by showing costs that still need testing.
It proves that a single summer gives a complete financial picture.
questions.explanation: The reviewer uses this episode to distinguish vivid imagery, practical constraints, measurable costs and sustained responsibility for waste.

questions.q: Which uncertainty would a school need to investigate before adopting the deposit scheme?
choices: How many cups will be lost or reused and what cleaning will cost.
Whether the shoreline looks clean in a film's final shot.
Whether the teenagers can borrow the exact same jugs again.
Whether the director will film the school event.
questions.explanation: The reviewer uses this episode to distinguish vivid imagery, practical constraints, measurable costs and sustained responsibility for waste.

questions.q: What does the reviewer most clearly want the audience to do after watching?
choices: Admire the final image without raising practical questions.
Discuss the routine work and responsibilities behind any change.
Replace school festivals with documentaries about beaches.
Assume that shame will be enough to change behaviour.
questions.explanation: The reviewer uses this episode to distinguish vivid imagery, practical constraints, measurable costs and sustained responsibility for waste.

questions.q: A pupil criticises classmates for not using reusable cups, even though they cannot bring them through security. How would the reviewer's reasoning challenge the criticism?
choices: Ask students to ignore the rules whenever the environmental goal is important.
Cancel all events until every guest owns a reusable cup.
Focus on a more dramatic picture of the problem.
Look at the constraints and find workable alternatives before assigning blame.
questions.explanation: The reviewer uses this episode to distinguish vivid imagery, practical constraints, measurable costs and sustained responsibility for waste.

questions.q: A festival committee says, 'Our cup system cost more this year, so it failed.' What response fits the review?
choices: Ignore expenses because environmental action cannot be measured.
Consider repeated use and longer-term costs before judging the result.
Conclude that reusable cups always cost less from the first day.
Treat the number of borrowed cups as the only relevant measure.
questions.explanation: The reviewer uses this episode to distinguish vivid imagery, practical constraints, measurable costs and sustained responsibility for waste.

questions.q: Which question would best continue the discussion the reviewer hopes the film will begin?
choices: Which shot of the coastline looked most beautiful on screen?
Could the director add a sadder soundtrack to the ending?
Can every individual promise never to make a mistake?
Who will maintain the bins, measure the costs and take responsibility next week?
questions.explanation: The reviewer uses this episode to distinguish vivid imagery, practical constraints, measurable costs and sustained responsibility for waste.
